Topic 01·Anik Sir · Lecture 1

Signals, energy and transformations

Continuous vs discrete, energy and power, shifting, reversing and scaling time, and even–odd parts.

5 past questions on this topic

What is a signal?

A signal is a pattern of change that carries information. The change can happen over time (a voice, a voltage, the speed of a car) or over space (the brightness of an image from pixel to pixel).

We write a signal as a function of an independent variable. In this course that variable is almost always called "time", even when it is really position.

Continuous and discrete signals

There are two kinds of time, and each has its own notation.

  • A continuous-time signal x(t)x(t)x(t) has a value at every real instant ttt. It is drawn as a smooth, unbroken curve. Examples: a microphone voltage, the temperature in a room, the velocity of a car.
  • A discrete-time signal x[n]x[n]x[n] has values only at integer instants n=…,−2,−1,0,1,2,…n=\dots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\dotsn=…,−2,−1,0,1,2,… Between samples there is nothing; the signal is not zero there, it is simply undefined. Examples: digital audio samples, a daily temperature log, a weekly stock index.

Convention. Round brackets mean continuous time, square brackets mean discrete time.

continuous x(t)x(t)x(t)discrete x[n]x[n]x[n]
allowed values of the variableany real tttintegers nnn only
meaningfulx(1)x(1)x(1), x(2)x(2)x(2), x(0.5)x(0.5)x(0.5), x(π)x(\pi)x(π)x[1]x[1]x[1], x[2]x[2]x[2]
meaningless—x[0.5]x[0.5]x[0.5], x[π]x[\pi]x[π]

Discrete signals often come from sampling a continuous one, x[n]=x(nTs)x[n]=x(nT_s)x[n]=x(nTs​), but they do not have to. A list of numbers is already a discrete signal.

How big is a signal? Energy

To measure the "size" of a signal, square its values and add them up. Squaring makes negative values count as much as positive ones, and the absolute value lets the same formula work for complex signals.

Energy over an interval:

E[t1,t2]=∫t1t2∣x(t)∣2 dtE[n1,n2]=∑n=n1n2∣x[n]∣2E_{[t_1,t_2]}=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}|x(t)|^2\,dt\qquad\qquad E_{[n_1,n_2]}=\sum_{n=n_1}^{n_2}|x[n]|^2E[t1​,t2​]​=∫t1​t2​​∣x(t)∣2dtE[n1​,n2​]​=n=n1​∑n2​​∣x[n]∣2

Total energy uses the whole time axis:

E∞=∫−∞∞∣x(t)∣2 dtE∞=∑n=−∞∞∣x[n]∣2E_\infty=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt\qquad\qquad E_\infty=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|x[n]|^2E∞​=∫−∞∞​∣x(t)∣2dtE∞​=n=−∞∑∞​∣x[n]∣2

x(t)={sin⁡t,0≤t≤π0,otherwisex(t)=\begin{cases}\sin t,&0\le t\le\pi\\0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}x(t)={sint,0,​0≤t≤πotherwise​

E=∣1∣2+∣−2∣2+∣2∣2+∣−1∣2=1+4+4+1=10.\begin{aligned}&E\\[6pt]&= |1|^2+|-2|^2+|2|^2+|-1|^2\\[6pt]&= 1+4+4+1\\[6pt]&= 10 .\end{aligned}​E=∣1∣2+∣−2∣2+∣2∣2+∣−1∣2=1+4+4+1=10.​

Power: energy per unit time

Power is energy averaged over the interval. Divide the energy by the length of the interval (continuous) or by the number of samples (discrete):

P[t1,t2]=1t2−t1∫t1t2∣x(t)∣2 dtP[n1,n2]=1n2−n1+1∑n=n1n2∣x[n]∣2P_{[t_1,t_2]}=\frac{1}{t_2-t_1}\int_{t_1}^{t_2}|x(t)|^2\,dt\qquad\qquad P_{[n_1,n_2]}=\frac{1}{n_2-n_1+1}\sum_{n=n_1}^{n_2}|x[n]|^2P[t1​,t2​]​=t2​−t1​1​∫t1​t2​​∣x(t)∣2dtP[n1​,n2​]​=n2​−n1​+11​n=n1​∑n2​​∣x[n]∣2

Note the +1+1+1 in the discrete case: from n1n_1n1​ to n2n_2n2​ there are n2−n1+1n_2-n_1+1n2​−n1​+1 samples.

Average power over all time is the limit as the interval grows:

P∞=lim⁡T→∞12T∫−TT∣x(t)∣2dtP∞=lim⁡N→∞12N+1∑n=−NN∣x[n]∣2P_\infty=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}|x(t)|^2dt\qquad\qquad P_\infty=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^{N}|x[n]|^2P∞​=T→∞lim​2T1​∫−TT​∣x(t)∣2dtP∞​=N→∞lim​2N+11​n=−N∑N​∣x[n]∣2

Back to the examples.

  • Half-sine: P[0,π]=π/2π−0=12P_{[0,\pi]}=\dfrac{\pi/2}{\pi-0}=\dfrac12P[0,π]​=π−0π/2​=21​. This is the average squared size over 0≤t≤π0\le t\le\pi0≤t≤π.
  • Four samples: P[0,3]=104=2.5P_{[0,3]}=\dfrac{10}{4}=2.5P[0,3]​=410​=2.5.

What if the half-sine repeats forever?

Now the half-sine repeats with period π\piπ: x(t)=∣sin⁡t∣x(t)=|\sin t|x(t)=∣sint∣.

  • Energy: every period contributes the same π/2\pi/2π/2, so E=π2+π2+π2+⋯=∞E=\frac\pi2+\frac\pi2+\frac\pi2+\cdots=\inftyE=2π​+2π​+2π​+⋯=∞.
  • Power: a periodic signal looks the same in every period, so averaging over one period is enough: P=1π∫0πsin⁡2t dt=1π⋅π2=12.\begin{aligned}&P\\[6pt]&= \frac1\pi\int_0^\pi\sin^2t\,dt\\[6pt]&= \frac1\pi\cdot\frac\pi2\\[6pt]&= \frac12 .\end{aligned}​P=π1​∫0π​sin2tdt=π1​⋅2π​=21​.​

If instead the lobe is followed by an equal rest, so the period becomes 2π2\pi2π, the energy per period is still π/2\pi/2π/2 but it is spread over twice the time:

E=∞,P=12π∫0πsin⁡2t dt=14.E=\infty,\qquad P=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\sin^2t\,dt=\frac14 .E=∞,P=2π1​∫0π​sin2tdt=41​.

Can a signal that never ends have finite energy?

Yes. Consider

x(t)={1,∣t∣≤11∣t∣,∣t∣>1x(t)=\begin{cases}1,&|t|\le1\\[2pt] \dfrac1{|t|},&|t|>1\end{cases}x(t)=⎩⎨⎧​1,∣t∣1​,​∣t∣≤1∣t∣>1​

E=∫−1112 dt+2∫1∞1t2 dt=2+2[−1t]1∞=2+2=4.\begin{aligned}&E\\[6pt]&= \int_{-1}^{1}1^2\,dt+2\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{t^2}\,dt\\[6pt]&= 2+2\left[-\frac1t\right]_1^\infty\\[6pt]&= 2+2\\[6pt]&= 4 .\end{aligned}​E=∫−11​12dt+2∫1∞​t21​dt=2+2[−t1​]1∞​=2+2=4.​

The total energy is finite, and when a finite amount of energy is spread over infinite time, the average power is P=0P=0P=0.

Every periodic signal (other than zero) is a power signal. Its power is the average over one period.

Transforming signals: vertical and horizontal changes

We often need to move, flip or stretch a signal. There are two very different kinds of change:

  • Vertical (amplitude) changes act on the value: 2x(t)2x(t)2x(t) doubles every value.
  • Horizontal (time) changes act on the time axis: x(2t)x(2t)x(2t) makes everything happen twice as fast.

The trick to reading horizontal changes: ask "when does the value that used to occur at t=at=at=a now occur?" In x(2t)x(2t)x(2t), the value A=x(a)A=x(a)A=x(a) appears when 2t=a2t=a2t=a, i.e. at t=a/2t=a/2t=a/2.

Time shift

y(t)=x(t−t0)y(t)=x(t-t_0)y(t)=x(t−t0​)

For t0>0t_0>0t0​>0:

  • x(t−t0)x(t-t_0)x(t−t0​) is a delay: the signal moves right by t0t_0t0​. Every value occurs t0t_0t0​ later.
  • x(t+t0)x(t+t_0)x(t+t0​) is an advance: the signal moves left by t0t_0t0​.

The height and shape do not change at all.

Why does "minus" move it right? The feature that was at t=at=at=a now needs t−t0=at-t_0=at−t0​=a, i.e. t=a+t0t=a+t_0t=a+t0​: later, so further right.

In discrete time, a shift moves every sample to a new index. x[n−4]x[n-4]x[n−4] is x[n]x[n]x[n] delayed by four samples. The shift must be an integer.

Time reversal

y(t)=x(−t)y(t)=x(-t)y(t)=x(−t)

Replace ttt by −t-t−t. The signal is mirrored about the vertical axis t=0t=0t=0: a feature at t=at=at=a appears at t=−at=-at=−a. It is like playing a recording backwards.

Time scaling

y(t)=x(at),a>0y(t)=x(at),\qquad a>0y(t)=x(at),a>0
  • a>1a>1a>1: compression. The signal happens faster and becomes narrower. x(2t)x(2t)x(2t) is half as wide.
  • 0<a<10<a<10<a<1: stretching. The signal happens slower and becomes wider. x(t/2)x(t/2)x(t/2) is twice as wide.

Scaling changes only the horizontal axis, not the height.

In discrete time scaling is delicate: x[2n]x[2n]x[2n] keeps only every other sample (information is lost), and x[n/2]x[n/2]x[n/2] is only defined when nnn is even.

Combining transformations

We can combine shifts, reversal and scaling, but the order matters. Each operation acts on the whole intermediate signal, replacing its time variable.

Goal: x(2t+3)x(2t+3)x(2t+3).

  • Shift left by 3: x(t)→x(t+3)x(t)\to x(t+3)x(t)→x(t+3).
  • Then compress by 2, i.e. replace ttt by 2t2t2t in x(t+3)x(t+3)x(t+3): x(2t+3)x(2t+3)x(2t+3). ✓

Reverse the order and you get something else:

  • Compress first: x(t)→x(2t)x(t)\to x(2t)x(t)→x(2t).
  • Then shift left by 3, i.e. replace ttt by t+3t+3t+3 in x(2t)x(2t)x(2t): x(2(t+3))=x(2t+6)x\big(2(t+3)\big)=x(2t+6)x(2(t+3))=x(2t+6). ✗

The shift got multiplied by 2.

A safe recipe for x(αt+β)x(\alpha t+\beta)x(αt+β)

  1. Shift first by β\betaβ: g1(t)=x(t+β)g_1(t)=x(t+\beta)g1​(t)=x(t+β). If β>0\beta>0β>0 shift left; if β<0\beta<0β<0 shift right.
  2. Reverse only if α<0\alpha<0α<0: g2(t)=g1(−t)g_2(t)=g_1(-t)g2​(t)=g1​(−t). Otherwise g2=g1g_2=g_1g2​=g1​.
  3. Scale by ∣α∣|\alpha|∣α∣: g3(t)=g2(∣α∣t)=x(αt+β)g_3(t)=g_2(|\alpha|t)=x(\alpha t+\beta)g3​(t)=g2​(∣α∣t)=x(αt+β). If ∣α∣>1|\alpha|>1∣α∣>1 compress; if 0<∣α∣<10<|\alpha|<10<∣α∣<1 stretch.

Always write the intermediate signal before applying the next step.

Worked example: x(−3t+2)x(-3t+2)x(−3t+2)

Start from

x(t)={1,0≤t<12−t,1≤t≤20,otherwisex(t)=\begin{cases}1,&0\le t<1\\ 2-t,&1\le t\le2\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}x(t)=⎩⎨⎧​1,2−t,0,​0≤t<11≤t≤2otherwise​

x(t+2)={1,−2≤t<−1−t,−1≤t≤00,otherwisex(t+2)=\begin{cases}1,&-2\le t<-1\\ -t,&-1\le t\le 0\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}x(t+2)=⎩⎨⎧​1,−t,0,​−2≤t<−1−1≤t≤0otherwise​

Step 2 — reverse (since α=−3<0\alpha=-3<0α=−3<0). Replace ttt by −t-t−t:

x(−t+2)={t,0≤t≤11,1<t≤20,otherwisex(-t+2)=\begin{cases}t,&0\le t\le1\\ 1,&1< t\le 2\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}x(−t+2)=⎩⎨⎧​t,1,0,​0≤t≤11<t≤2otherwise​

Step 3 — compress by 3. Replace ttt by 3t3t3t; the signal becomes three times narrower:

x(−3t+2)={3t,0≤t≤131,13<t≤230,otherwisex(-3t+2)=\begin{cases}3t,&0\le t\le\frac13\\ 1,&\frac13< t\le\frac23\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}x(−3t+2)=⎩⎨⎧​3t,1,0,​0≤t≤31​31​<t≤32​otherwise​

Check with a single point. The corner of x(t)x(t)x(t) at t=1t=1t=1 (where the flat part ends) must appear where −3t+2=1-3t+2=1−3t+2=1, i.e. t=13t=\frac13t=31​. ✓

Practice 2

Start with y0(t)=x(t)y_0(t)=x(t)y0​(t)=x(t) and apply, in this order: stretch by 2, shift left by 3, compress by 4, reverse.

Solution. Each step replaces ttt in the previous signal:

y1(t)=x ⁣(t2),y2(t)=y1(t+3)=x ⁣(t+32),y_1(t)=x\!\left(\tfrac t2\right),\quad y_2(t)=y_1(t+3)=x\!\left(\tfrac{t+3}{2}\right),y1​(t)=x(2t​),y2​(t)=y1​(t+3)=x(2t+3​), \end{aligned}$$ > **Fast check for any combination.** In $x(\alpha t+\beta)$, a feature of $x$ at $t_0$ appears at $t=\dfrac{t_0-\beta}{\alpha}$. Map every corner and jump this way, then join the dots. ## Even and odd signals - **Even:** $x(-t)=x(t)$. The graph is a mirror image about the vertical axis. Example: $\cos t$. - **Odd:** $x(-t)=-x(t)$. The graph flips sign across the origin. Example: $\sin t$. An odd signal must have $x(0)=0$, because $x(0)=-x(0)$. ```fig sig-even-odd ``` Useful facts: - even × even = even, odd × odd = even, even × odd = odd; - $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}\text{(odd)}\,dt=0$ and $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}\text{(even)}\,dt=2\int_0^a\text{(even)}\,dt$. ## Every signal has an even part and an odd part Any signal, even one that is neither even nor odd, can be split as $x=x_e+x_o$ with

x_e(t)=\frac12\big[x(t)+x(-t)\big],\qquad x_o(t)=\frac12\big[x(t)-x(-t)\big].

**Three quick checks** that this works: 1. $x_e$ is even: $x_e(-t)=\frac12[x(-t)+x(t)]=x_e(t)$. 2. $x_o$ is odd: $x_o(-t)=\frac12[x(-t)-x(t)]=-x_o(t)$. 3. They add up: $x_e+x_o=\frac12[x(t)+x(-t)]+\frac12[x(t)-x(-t)]=x(t)$. ### Continuous example

x(t)=\begin{cases}t+1,&-1\le t\le1\0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

This is neither even nor odd. Reflect it: for $-1\le t\le1$, $x(-t)=-t+1=1-t$. - **Even part** (add, then average): $x_e(t)=\frac12\big[(t+1)+(1-t)\big]=1$ for $|t|\le1$. - **Odd part** (subtract, then average): $x_o(t)=\frac12\big[(t+1)-(1-t)\big]=t$ for $|t|\le1$. ```fig sig-eo-ct ``` ### Discrete example: the unit step

x[n]=u[n]=\begin{cases}1,&n\ge0\0,&n<0\end{cases}\qquad x[-n]=\begin{cases}1,&n\le0\0,&n>0\end{cases}

x_e[n]=\tfrac12\big(x[n]+x[-n]\big)=\begin{cases}1,&n=0\ \tfrac12,&n\ne0\end{cases}\qquad x_o[n]=\tfrac12\big(x[n]-x[-n]\big)=\begin{cases}-\tfrac12,&n<0\ 0,&n=0\ \tfrac12,&n>0\end{cases}

```fig sig-eo-dt ``` **Recipe for piece-wise signals:** write out $x(-t)$ piece by piece, line up the intervals, then add or subtract interval by interval. Check that $x_o(0)=0$ and that $x_e+x_o$ gives back $x$. ## Exam pointers - For any $x(\alpha t+\beta)$ question, make a small table: interval of the argument → interval of $t$ → expression. State the property used at each step (shift, reversal, scaling). - Energy or power: first decide whether the integral (or sum) converges. If $E$ is finite, $P=0$; if the signal is periodic, compute $P$ over one period. - Even–odd decomposition: show $x(-t)$ explicitly, then both formulas, then the checks.
